items.headline: Army awards up to $2.2bn across five bases for microreactors
items.what_happened: The Army signed milestone-based Other Transaction Authority agreements worth up to $2.2 billion combined, running FY2027-FY2031, with five companies to build and operate microreactors: Antares at Fort Bragg, Radiant at Fort Benning, BWXT at Fort Campbell, General Atomics at Fort Hood, and Westinghouse Government Services at Fort Drum. Only Radiant disclosed its own award value, up to $750 million for 15 Kaleidos units; the Army declined to break out the other four. The five installations were narrowed down from a longer list of nine candidate sites that the Army and the Defense Innovation Unit identified in November 2025.
items.why_it_matters: This is the largest concentrated public bet on the microreactor class to date, and the Army's own program lead was candid that nobody knows what these reactors will actually cost and that some of the five vendors will likely fail before 2028 — the government is explicitly underwriting first-of-a-kind construction risk rather than waiting for a market price to form.
items.binding_note: Each vendor holds a signed, executed OTA agreement, not a preliminary selection — funds release against technical milestones for prototype construction and a first year of operation, after which the Army plans to shift to a power purchase agreement. Per-vendor dollar figures beyond Radiant's remain undisclosed.

items.headline: Antares to build three R1 microreactors at Fort Bragg
items.what_happened: The Army selected Antares Nuclear to own, build and operate a three-unit R1 deployment at Fort Bragg, home of the XVIII Airborne Corps, under Janus. Antares declined to disclose the contract's value but said its combined book across Janus, the Air Force ANPI award at Joint Base San Antonio, and Space Force work is now on the order of $1 billion. The R1 units, 100 kWe-1 MWe sodium heat-pipe reactors fueled by TRISO, build on the company's Mark-0 test reactor, which reached criticality at Idaho National Laboratory on June 4, 2026.
items.why_it_matters: Antares is now a three-program vendor (Janus, ANPI, Space Force) without a single disclosed contract value for any of them, so the $1 billion figure is entirely self-reported — a case study in how thin the public paper trail is even for a company winning federal reactor work.
items.binding_note: A signed Janus OTA agreement, not a mere selection; the dollar value of this specific award is undisclosed, only the combined cross-program total.

items.headline: Radiant wins largest Janus award, up to $750M for 15 units
items.what_happened: Radiant secured the largest of the five Janus awards, up to $750 million to develop and deploy 15 Kaleidos microreactors across Army installations by 2030, starting with a three-unit deployment at Fort Benning targeted for 2028. Radiant called it one of the largest contracts ever issued through the Defense Innovation Unit. The award adds to Radiant's existing Air Force ANPI selection at Buckley Space Force Base and its commercial Equinix agreement for 20 Kaleidos units.
items.why_it_matters: A single award now covers three quarters of the Janus program's disclosed dollar figure and 15 of its 20-plus planned units, meaning the program's near-term commercial track record will be dominated by one vendor and one reactor design.
items.binding_note: Radiant itself described this as a binding Janus agreement, the only one of the five vendors to publish its own award ceiling.

items.headline: BWXT to deploy 20 MWe BANR reactor at Fort Campbell
items.what_happened: BWXT Advanced Technologies will deploy a 20 MWe (75 MWth) configuration of its BANR high-temperature gas reactor at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, the largest single reactor in the Janus program. BWXT did not disclose the contract's value but confirmed a phased structure, with groundbreaking targeted for late 2028 and operation in the early 2030s. The design scales up BWXT's 1.5 MWe Project Pele microreactor, which delivered a full TRISO fuel core to the Department of Defense in late 2025.
items.why_it_matters: BWXT is the only Janus vendor that fabricates its own TRISO fuel, at its NRC-licensed Lynchburg, Virginia plant, which also supplies fuel to Antares and Radiant — making it a supplier to its own Janus competitors as well as a reactor vendor in its own right.
items.binding_note: A signed Janus OTA agreement; the specific dollar value was not disclosed.

items.headline: General Atomics to advance GA-TES microreactor at Fort Hood
items.what_happened: General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems will advance its GA-TES microreactor at Fort Hood, Texas through development, testing and site-planning milestones; the award's value was not disclosed. GA-TES is the only Janus reactor that does not use TRISO fuel — it runs on uranium-zirconium hydride drawing on General Atomics' TRIGA research-reactor heritage, is liquid-metal-cooled with natural circulation, and has a baseline output of about 5 MWe scalable to roughly 20 MWe. GA-EMS did not name a fuel supplier or utility partner for the site.
items.why_it_matters: GA-TES is the least mature of the five Janus designs by disclosed detail, and it is also the only one using a fuel form other than TRISO, so its supply chain and licensing path diverge from the rest of the program's four TRISO-based vendors.
items.binding_note: A signed Janus OTA agreement covering development and testing milestones, not yet a deployment commitment; the company is explicitly in a development phase.

items.headline: Westinghouse to bring eVinci to Fort Drum after Schumer push
items.what_happened: The Army selected Westinghouse Government Services to deploy its eVinci heat-pipe microreactor at Fort Drum, New York, home of the 10th Mountain Division; Westinghouse did not disclose output, schedule or contract value. POWER reported the selection followed a mid-August letter from Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to Army Secretary Dan Driscoll urging that Fort Drum be prioritized. Westinghouse is also the ANPI selectee at Malmstrom Air Force Base, Montana.
items.why_it_matters: This is a rare documented case of a named senator lobbying directly for a specific base's inclusion in a reactor siting decision, and it landed — worth watching whether other undisclosed sites got the same treatment without a public paper trail.
items.binding_note: A signed Janus OTA agreement, not a mere selection, though none of output, schedule or value has been disclosed for this specific pairing.

items.headline: Westinghouse eVinci reaches zero-power criticality in Nevada
items.what_happened: Westinghouse's eVinci microreactor design achieved zero-power criticality at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center, a National Nuclear Security Administration facility at the Nevada National Security Site, at 10:39 a.m. Pacific on August 24, 2026, two days before the Janus announcement named Westinghouse for Fort Drum. The test was completed in partnership with Los Alamos National Laboratory and Idaho National Laboratory.
items.why_it_matters: This is a genuine technical milestone, not a business announcement, and its timing two days ahead of a $2.2 billion Army award is a reminder that a company's demonstrated hardware progress and its federal contract wins are moving on separate, only loosely coordinated tracks.
items.binding_note: An achieved physical milestone (criticality), independently confirmed, not a company claim or a forward-looking target.

items.headline: Radiant locks in Standard Nuclear TRISO fabrication through 2031
items.what_happened: Radiant and Standard Nuclear announced a binding, multi-metric-ton TRISO fuel fabrication agreement extending through 2031. DOE-allocated HALEU will supply the enriched uranium; Standard Nuclear fabricates it into reactor-ready TRISO particle fuel for Kaleidos units under both the Janus and ANPI programs. Radiant said the agreement covers a distinct risk from HALEU access itself — the specialized fabrication capacity needed to turn allocated material into qualified fuel.
items.why_it_matters: Fuel fabrication capacity, not enrichment, is the supply-chain bottleneck this deal targets directly — a vendor can hold a HALEU allocation and still have nowhere to turn it into qualified fuel, and this agreement is Radiant buying its way out of that specific risk through the early 2030s.
items.binding_note: Described by Radiant as a binding, multi-metric-ton agreement with a fixed end date, not an MOU or exploratory arrangement.

items.headline: Antares signs Standard Nuclear TRISO deal, options more through 2035
items.what_happened: Antares announced a binding agreement under which Standard Nuclear will supply 1 metric ton of TRISO fuel, with Antares holding an option for up to seven additional metric tons through 2035. Antares had previously said it expected to source TRISO from both Standard Nuclear and BWXT, but has not disclosed a binding agreement with BWXT. The company has not said how much of the Standard Nuclear fuel will support Janus, ANPI, or its Space Force work.
items.why_it_matters: Coming one day after the Janus awards and one week after Radiant's own Standard Nuclear deal, this shows fuel fabrication capacity is becoming a real point of competition between microreactor vendors, not just a shared industry dependency.
items.binding_note: The initial 1 metric ton supply is a binding agreement; the additional seven metric tons are an option, not a commitment.

items.headline: Antares Mark-0 becomes first Reactor Pilot Program reactor to go critical
items.what_happened: Antares' Mark-0 test reactor achieved zero-power fueled criticality at Idaho National Laboratory on June 4, 2026, becoming the first company in the DOE's Reactor Pilot Program to hit the milestone. Mark-0 is a forerunner to the company's flagship R1 sodium heat-pipe, TRISO-fueled microreactor and is configured for criticality testing only, without power conversion or heat removal systems. The milestone came exactly one month before the July 4, 2026 deadline set by Executive Order 14301 for at least three RPP reactors to reach criticality.
items.why_it_matters: This was the opening move in what became a five-company race to and past the July 4 deadline, and Antares' head start put it ahead of four other companies that would also cross the line before summer's end.
items.binding_note: An achieved, DOE-authorized physical milestone, not a target or a company claim.

items.headline: Valar Atomics reactor reaches criticality at Utah test site
items.what_happened: Valar Atomics' Ward 250 helium-cooled, TRISO-fueled reactor reached zero-power fueled criticality on June 18, 2026 at the Utah San Rafael Energy Lab, where the company broke ground in September 2025. ANS described the criticality test as 100 kWt; DOE's April NEPA record describes the proposed Ward250 research facility as 250 kWt. The public sources do not explain the difference, so this record does not choose a single rating. It was the second of what became five companies to reach DOE-authorized criticality ahead of the Reactor Pilot Program's July 4 deadline, following Antares Nuclear. The reactor had earlier reached a separate zero-power criticality milestone in a November 2025 test called Nova Core, run with Los Alamos National Laboratory at the Nevada Criticality Experiments Research Center.
items.why_it_matters: A second company crossing the line within two weeks of the first showed the July 4 target was an achievable bar for multiple independent designs and teams, not a stretch goal for a single frontrunner.
items.binding_note: An achieved, DOE-authorized physical milestone.

items.headline: Valar powers an Nvidia chip, announces 30 MW Utah data center
items.what_happened: On June 22, 2026, Valar Atomics announced it had achieved a 10 kWt power ascension with its Ward 250 reactor, converted that output to electricity, and connected it to an Nvidia Spark chip. The demonstration was paired with a broader announcement that Valar and Nvidia are partnering to develop a 30 MW data center in Utah.
items.why_it_matters: This is a rare case of a company actually closing the loop from reactor to a named chip rather than describing a future data-center customer in the abstract, though the 30 MW data center itself remains a partnership announcement, not a signed offtake agreement.
items.binding_note: The power-ascension test is a real achieved milestone, but the 30 MW data center is described only as a partnership at this stage, with no PPA or construction commitment disclosed.

items.headline: Deployable Energy reactor goes critical about 150 days after start
items.what_happened: Deployable Energy's 1 MWe Unity microreactor, a high-temperature gas-cooled design, reached zero-power fueled criticality at Idaho National Laboratory on June 30, 2026, about 150 days after the company began the project; it announced the milestone July 1 under the DOE's Nuclear Energy Launch Pad program. Deployable Energy had only recently emerged from stealth, and little about its broader plans is public beyond stated work with partners in Utah and Texas on data centers, research facilities and remote resource extraction.
items.why_it_matters: Going from project start to criticality in roughly five months, faster than any other company in the program, is the strongest evidence that the DOE's compressed authorization pathway can compress timelines for a genuinely new entrant, not only for companies with years of prior reactor work.
items.binding_note: An achieved, DOE-authorized physical milestone.

items.headline: Aalo Atomics hits criticality at 12:20 a.m. on deadline day
items.what_happened: Aalo Atomics' Aalo-X Critical Test Reactor, nicknamed Project First Light, reached zero-power fueled criticality at 12:20 a.m. Mountain time on July 4, 2026 at Idaho National Laboratory — the fourth company to hit the milestone and the last to do so before the Executive Order 14301 deadline expired that same day. DOE said the reactor went from groundbreaking to a sustained chain reaction in under eight months. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the department had been asked to deliver three reactors by America's 250th anniversary and delivered four.
items.why_it_matters: Landing at 12:20 a.m. on the deadline date itself is about as close as a federal target can be cut, and it means the administration's three-reactor goal was exceeded by exactly one company with hours to spare, not weeks.
items.binding_note: An achieved, DOE-authorized physical milestone.

items.headline: Oklo secures DOE safety approval for its Aurora-INL reactor
items.what_happened: Oklo announced on June 11, 2026 that it had secured preliminary documented safety analysis (PDSA) approval from the DOE for Aurora-INL, its planned first deployment of the 75 MWe Aurora Powerhouse liquid-metal-cooled fast reactor. Oklo broke ground on Aurora-INL in September 2025 and has not published a criticality or completion timeline for the project. Oklo is the only company with two separate Reactor Pilot Program projects — Aurora-INL and a plutonium-fueled fast test reactor called Pluto — plus a third, isotope-focused project run through its Oklo Isotopes subsidiary.
items.why_it_matters: A PDSA is one authorization step short of the documented safety analysis needed to operate, making this real progress on Oklo's actual commercial reactor design, distinct from the isotope test reactor that generated its criticality headlines two months later.
items.binding_note: A DOE regulatory approval actually granted (PDSA), not merely applied for.

items.headline: Oklo's isotope test reactor becomes fifth to reach criticality
items.what_happened: Oklo's Groves Isotope Test Reactor, a 15 MWt pool-type reactor in Lockhart, Texas built through the company's Oklo Isotopes subsidiary, achieved criticality on the night of August 5-6, 2026 — the fifth DOE-authorized advanced reactor to do so in 2026, more than a month after the July 4 deadline had already been met by four other companies. DOE said Oklo built Groves from a greenfield site on private land, completing civil construction, procurement and fuel loading in under a year. The reactor is intended to inform a future commercial isotope-production variant for medical and industrial use, not electricity generation.
items.why_it_matters: This is the clearest evidence that the July 4 deadline was a floor, not a ceiling — the DOE-authorized pathway kept producing criticality milestones for months afterward, and this one is also the program's first isotope-production, rather than power, reactor.
items.binding_note: An achieved, DOE-authorized physical milestone.

items.headline: DOE names eight newcomers in second Launch Pad selection round
items.what_happened: The National Reactor Innovation Center at Idaho National Laboratory selected 13 projects across 12 companies for the second round of the Nuclear Energy Launch Pad program on August 25, 2026. Eight of the twelve are newcomers not previously part of the Reactor Pilot Program or Launch Pad: Atlas Atomics, Forge Atomics, Hexium, Lightbridge, Nusano, Raven-Flint Nuclear, Scaled Atomics, and Sublime Atomics. The other four selectees — Antares Nuclear, Deployable Energy, Oklo, and Valar Atomics — were already among the five companies that had achieved DOE-authorized criticality that summer; Aalo Atomics, the fifth, was not part of this round.
items.why_it_matters: Doubling the roster of DOE-track reactor companies just seven weeks after the July 4 deadline shows the government treating its pilot program as a success story to scale up rather than a one-time push, putting eight new companies on the same accelerated path that took the first group from groundbreaking to criticality in months.
items.binding_note: A program selection granting access to DOE technical, regulatory and testing support — the first step toward signing an OTA, per the program's own four-step process — not itself a construction or purchase commitment.

items.headline: Last Energy clears DOE safety review for its PWR-5 pilot
items.what_happened: The DOE approved Last Energy's preliminary documented safety analysis (PDSA) for its PWR-5 pilot reactor at the Texas A&M RELLIS campus, reported May 29, 2026. PWR-5 is a scaled-down demonstration version of Last Energy's commercial 20 MWe PWR-20 design. The company had already begun construction at RELLIS and said it had completed the pilot building and installed reactor components; it has since submitted its final documented safety analysis and expected an initial criticality test in summer 2026 pending DOE authorization.
items.why_it_matters: PWR-5 is explicitly a bridge reactor built to de-risk the PWR-20 commercial design, so DOE clearing its safety case is a proxy signal for how the agency will treat Last Energy's actual 30-unit Haskell County plant later.
items.binding_note: A DOE regulatory approval actually granted (PDSA), not merely applied for.

items.headline: Natura Resources signs HALEU supply agreement with Quadrant Nuclear
items.what_happened: Natura Resources announced a formal agreement on June 11, 2026 to receive HALEU fuel from Quadrant Nuclear Industries (QNI), a startup building a downblending and reprocessing facility at Idaho National Laboratory designed to produce up to 18 metric tons of HALEU annually. The companies said the deal establishes a framework toward a long-term offtake arrangement, not a completed one. Natura's liquid-fueled molten salt reactor design can draw HALEU from a wider range of source materials than solid-fuel designs, including reprocessed highly enriched uranium.
items.why_it_matters: This is a second named buyer for a HALEU source that does not yet exist commercially — QNI's Idaho reprocessing facility is still in development — showing microreactor vendors pre-committing to fuel supply that is itself unproven at scale.
items.binding_note: Described by both companies as a step toward a future long-term offtake framework, not a completed supply contract with committed volumes or a price.

items.headline: Aalo Atomics locks in fuel rods from Global Nuclear Fuel
items.what_happened: Aalo Atomics signed a fuel fabrication contract with Global Nuclear Fuel (GNF), a GE Vernova-Hitachi alliance, announced March 3, 2026. GNF is fabricating uranium dioxide fuel rods from low-enriched uranium into assemblies for the Aalo-X test reactor; that same month Aalo said Urenco USA had finished enriching the feedstock and delivered it to GNF. Aalo separately contracted Baker Hughes for a 10 MWe steam turbine generator set for the same reactor.

items.headline: NRC finalizes Part 53, its first new reactor rule in decades
items.what_happened: The NRC voted to finalize 10 CFR Part 53, "Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Regulatory Framework for Advanced Reactors," on March 26, 2026, with an effective date of April 29, 2026. It is the first new US reactor licensing framework in more than 30 years and arrives over a year ahead of the end-of-2027 deadline set by the 2019 Nuclear Energy Innovation and Modernization Act. Part 53 is optional and does not replace the existing Part 50/52 pathways; it adds technology-inclusive safety standards, risk-based design flexibility, and graded security requirements alongside them.
items.why_it_matters: Part 53 is the general-purpose advanced-reactor framework; the NRC's own chairman said on the same call that a separate microreactor-specific rule was still coming, which arrived five weeks later as Part 57 — Part 53 is the foundation the microreactor-specific fast lane was built on top of.
items.binding_note: A finalized, effective federal rule, not a proposal.

items.headline: NRC proposes Part 57 fast lane for microreactor licensing
items.what_happened: The NRC announced a proposed rule, 10 CFR Part 57, on April 24, 2026, creating a streamlined licensing pathway specifically for microreactors and other reactors with comparable risk profiles, with a Federal Register notice tentatively scheduled for May 6. The agency and industry estimate the framework could save $3.76 billion to $11.84 billion sector-wide, largely by reducing exemption requests, and could shrink construction-permit and operating-license timelines to six months to a year. Part 57 allows fleet approval of identical reactor designs, alternative design standards for novel reactors, streamlined environmental review, and limited construction before a permit is issued; it follows the earlier-2026 creation of a dedicated NRC Office of Advanced Reactors under Jeremy S. Bowen.
items.why_it_matters: This is the regulatory answer to the exact problem every microreactor vendor in this dataset has: a design that doesn't fit light-water-reactor rules and a business model built on building the same unit dozens of times, which the traditional one-off licensing process was never built to price or schedule.
items.binding_note: A proposed rule out for comment, not yet final or in effect.

items.headline: Texas opens $350M nuclear fund, but few projects qualify yet
items.what_happened: The Texas Advanced Nuclear Energy Office opened applications on April 1, 2026 for $350 million from the Texas Advanced Nuclear Development Fund, created by 2025's H.B. 14, through two reimbursement programs for construction and supply-chain projects. To qualify, an applicant must already have, or reasonably expect to have, a docketed NRC construction permit or license application by December 1, 2026. TANEO director Jarred Shaffer said only two projects in the state currently clear that bar, and both are utility-scale designs (Dow/X-energy's Xe-100 and Fermi America's AP1000s at the Pantex site), not microreactors. Abilene Christian University's Natura Resources molten salt research reactor holds a docketed NRC permit but is excluded from the construction program because it already received $120 million from other state funding.
items.why_it_matters: A fund explicitly framed around advanced nuclear and supply-chain manufacturing currently has zero eligible microreactor projects, and the one Texas microreactor project with an actual NRC docket is locked out by a rule against double-dipping state money — the headline dollar figure and the near-term reality for microreactor vendors are two different stories.

items.headline: NRC grants Kairos a 28-month delay on Hermes 1 reactor
items.what_happened: The NRC approved Kairos Power's request to extend the construction completion deadline for its Hermes 1 demonstration reactor in Oak Ridge, Tennessee by 28 months, from December 31, 2026 to April 30, 2029, reported April 22, 2026. It is a useful baseline for how long first-of-a-kind advanced-reactor construction actually takes when the DOE shortcuts are not in play.

items.headline: GAO flags uncertain HALEU demand for defense microreactors
items.what_happened: The Government Accountability Office published a report to Congress on August 25, 2026, "Nuclear Fuel: Actions Needed to Enhance Cost Reporting and Economic Analysis for Federal Uranium Supply Efforts," reviewing NNSA and DOE enriched-uranium planning. Among its unclassified findings, GAO identified a potential future demand stream for unobligated HALEU for microreactors under development for Department of Defense use, but said commercial and defense HALEU demand estimates remain highly uncertain because it is unclear how many of the more than 15 advanced reactor designs now in NRC licensing will actually be proven, ordered, and deployed. GAO issued five recommendations, including that DOE analyze whether its funding to expand LEU and HALEU enrichment capacity is actually inducing the production growth it is meant to induce.
items.why_it_matters: This is a government watchdog, not a critic or a competitor, saying out loud what every fuel-supply deal in this dataset implicitly assumes: nobody yet knows how much HALEU the microreactor industry will actually need, because nobody yet knows how many of these companies' reactors will actually get built.
items.binding_note: A published GAO report to Congress, an actual government finding, though its recommendations are advisory and not self-executing.

items.headline: State AGs call NRC's microreactor fast-track rule illegal
items.what_happened: California Attorney General Rob Bonta led a coalition of state attorneys general in a June 16, 2026 comment letter to the NRC opposing the proposed Part 57 microreactor licensing rule, arguing it violates the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act by skirting environmental review for a class of reactors the coalition called largely untested and experimental. The letter came at the close of Part 57's public comment period, which the NRC had opened May 1, 2026 under Executive Order 14300's direction to revise NRC regulations. The states asked the NRC to conduct a full NEPA review of the foreseeable environmental impacts of fleets of microreactors before finalizing any rule.
items.why_it_matters: This is the direct legal counterweight to every regulatory item in this dataset praising Part 57's speed — a coalition of state attorneys general is on record calling the same rule illegal, which means Part 57 is very likely to face litigation if and when it is finalized, adding real legal risk to every vendor counting on its 6-12 month licensing timeline.
items.binding_note: An actual filed comment letter taking a legal position, not a rumor of opposition — though it is advocacy against a not-yet-final rule, not a lawsuit or a court ruling.

items.headline: Air Force airlifts Valar's reactor components to Utah
items.what_happened: Three U.S. Air Force C-17s carried components of Valar Atomics' Ward 250 test reactor from March Air Reserve Base, California to Hill Air Force Base near Layton, Utah on Sunday, February 15, 2026, for onward delivery to the San Rafael Energy Lab. The event was attended by DOE Secretary Chris Wright, Utah Governor Spencer Cox, Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey, and Sen. John Curtis. Officials said the reactor was expected to be switched on by July 4, a target Valar met, reaching criticality on June 18.
items.why_it_matters: This is the physical, load-bearing proof behind every microreactor vendor's claim about factory-built, transportable reactors: a real reactor's components moving by military cargo plane, four months before the machine actually went critical, with three federal officials and the state's governor showing up to watch it land.
items.binding_note: An actual, completed physical transport, not a rendering or a plan.
